title: H-1B and L-1 Visa Extension Fees Jump by Thousands Starting September 9
excerpt: Employers with large H-1B and L-1 workforces will pay an additional $4,000 to $4,500 per extension petition under an expanded DHS rule taking effect next month.
body:
• Starting September 9, 2026, the 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee will apply to all H-1B and L-1 visa extension petitions, not just initial filings and employer changes.
  • The fee is $4,000 per H-1B extension and $4,500 per L-1 extension, payable by the employer, not the visa holder.
  • Only companies with 50 or more U.S. employees, where more than half the workforce holds H-1B or L-1 status, are subject to the surcharge.
  • The expansion comes on top of steep premium processing fee hikes that took effect in March 2026, raising costs for H-1B petitions from $2,805 to $2,965.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security will begin collecting an expanded biometric surcharge on H-1B and L-1 visa extension petitions starting September 9, 2026 — a move that will add thousands of dollars to the cost of retaining foreign workers already employed in the United States.

Under the finalized rule, the 9/11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee — currently $4,000 for H-1B petitions and $4,500 for L-1 petitions — will now apply to same-employer extension requests. Previously, DHS only collected the fee on initial petitions and change-of-employer filings.

Who Pays and How Much

The surcharge applies exclusively to employers meeting two thresholds: at least 50 employees based in the United States, and more than 50 percent of that workforce holding H-1B or L-1 visa status. The employer, not the visa holder, must pay the fee.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2087916763568849045

For qualifying companies, every routine three-year H-1B extension will now carry an additional $4,000 charge on top of existing filing fees. L-1 intracompany transferee extensions will cost an extra $4,500. The requirement applies to petitions filed through September 30, 2027.

"DHS is proposing to significantly change its interpretation regarding when the 9-11 Biometric Fee is required."

— American Immigration Lawyers Association

A Broader Pattern of Rising Costs

The expansion arrives amid a wave of visa fee increases affecting Indian professionals and their employers. In March 2026, USCIS raised premium processing fees for Form I-129 petitions — used for H-1B, L-1, and O-1 visas — from $2,805 to $2,965. The agency also shifted premium processing timelines from 15 calendar days to 15 business days, effectively adding a week to expedited decisions.

These changes build on the April 2024 overhaul that raised the base H-1B petition filing fee by nearly 70 percent, from $460 to $780 for large employers. Small businesses with 25 or fewer employees continue to pay the reduced $460 rate.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration's $100,000 supplemental fee on new H-1B petitions — announced in September 2025 — was struck down by U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin on June 8, 2026, who ruled it constituted an unlawful tax not authorized by Congress. A federal appeals court in Boston subsequently refused the government's motion to stay that ruling, keeping the $100,000 fee blocked for now.

Impact on Indian Tech Workers

India-born professionals account for more than 70 percent of all approved H-1B petitions annually, making any fee change disproportionately significant for the Indian diaspora. IT services firms that rely heavily on H-1B and L-1 workers to staff U.S. projects — many of which meet the 50-employee, 50-percent threshold — will face the steepest cost increases.

DHS says the additional revenue will fund its congressional mandate to build and maintain a comprehensive biometric entry-exit system at U.S. ports of entry. The agency estimates the expansion will roughly double collections from the 9/11 fee, increasing H-1B-related revenue from $68 million to approximately $129 million annually.

What's Next

Employers sponsoring H-1B and L-1 workers should review upcoming extension timelines against the September 9 effective date. Immigration attorneys recommend filing extension petitions before that date where possible to avoid the additional charge. Companies not meeting the 50-employee, 50-percent threshold remain unaffected.

The American Immigration Lawyers Association has opposed the expanded interpretation, arguing it contradicts the statute's original intent and imposes significant additional costs on employers who are already paying fraud detection fees for initial petitions.
